catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q2.explanation: D - designedThe only other verb that collocated well with ‘scheme’ is ‘propose’. However, it is not used with the preposition ‘to’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q3.explanation: B - freesThis is the only verb that collocates with ‘from’ preposition.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q4.explanation: C - exposureOnce again, exposure is the sole noun that can be used with ‘to’ preposition that follows it.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q5.explanation: D - involvesAnswers A and B do not fit here contextually. Answer C could be used if it weren‘t for ‘making’ that follows the gap.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q6.explanation: C - set upThe meaning of this phrasal verb is ‘founded or established’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q7.explanation: B - aimHe is aiming to. Other options have different meanings and do not fit the sentence.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-1-q8.explanation: D - indicationsIndications are visible signs of something that is happening. B and C have different meaning. The word ‘signals’ implies less obvious evidence, whereas in this case we are talking about explicit, more obvious results.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q9.explanation: from/withA straightforward gap with some leeway in meaning

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q10.explanation: whichAn example of a relative clause.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q11.explanation: theirEven though ‘everyone’ is considered to be singular, ‘their’ is used to mean both men and women and generally to follow the formal register of the text.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q12.explanation: doThe verb we need here should relate to the previously used ‘adopts’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q13.explanation: as‘To regard as’ means ‘to consider, to believe to be something’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q14.explanation: bring‘To bring to life’ = to liven up, to make look brighter and alive.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q15.explanation: must/shouldThe modality of the verb doesn’t change the meaning of the saying dramatically, so both modals can be used.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-2-q16.explanation: it/thisJust like in the previous case, both pronouns fit this gap.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q17.explanation: inhabitedA verb is needed here. Pay attention to the verb-forming prefix ‘in’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q18.explanation: heightBe careful not to misspell the word. See the list of words with difficult spelling.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q19.explanation: descendantAnother word that could be easily misspelled. Pay attention to the suffix -ant, spelled with an ‘a’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q20.explanation: mountainousAn adjective meaning ‘covered by mountain ranges’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q21.explanation: findingsCapitalisation doesn’t really matter here as all the letters in your answer sheet are going to be capitals. Make sure to pluralise the word though on the account of ‘have’ referring to the plural form.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q22.explanation: originatedA past simple form of the verb is important here because the text states a definite period of time in the past.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q23.explanation: adaptationsA biology term that means changes that happen to fit better into the environment the living thing exists in.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-3-q24.explanation: storageNote that ‘storing’ doesn’t fit very well – it would fit better had it preceded the word ‘fat’ in this context.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q25.explanation: The formal phrase “on receipt of” is replaced with the more common time conjunction “as soon as.” The passive construction “will be despatched” changes to the active “will despatch,” and “receipt” (noun) becomes “receive” (verb). The structure is “as soon as + subject + present simple” to refer to the future.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q26.explanation: This is a third conditional sentence, used to imagine a different past. The real situation (the gym increased fees) is reversed. The phrasal verb “put up” means “increase.” The negative form “had not put up” is required. Note the inversion: “If the gym had not put up…” is correct.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q27.explanation: The verb “delayed” becomes the noun “delay.” The active verb “had broken down” becomes the noun “breakdown.” The passive structure “was caused by” connects the two nouns. The possessive “our” is used with “delay” to maintain the meaning.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q28.answer: it been for Sarah’s; for Sarah’s
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q28.explanation: The fixed expression “if it had not been for” is used to say that one person or thing was essential to a past situation. It is the third conditional equivalent of “thanks to” or “because of.” Note the past perfect subjunctive form (“had been”).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q29.answer: with the exception of Leo came
catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q29.explanation: The phrase “with the exception of” is used to mean “except.” The sentence is reorganized so that “everyone” becomes the subject, and Leo is the exception. The verb “came” must agree with “everyone” (singular).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-4-q30.explanation: “Should have started” expresses an expectation about the past. This is replaced by “was due to start,” which means it was scheduled or expected to begin. The structure is “was/were due to + infinitive.”

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-5-q31.explanation: BSentence two of the first paragraph openly invites us to look at the data that supports the popular idea of newspapers being doomed. The remaining part of the paragraph presents facts and figures to substantiate this claim. Answer A is wrong – the author gives no interpretation of the trend, but instead believes that it is impossible to accurately predict the future of print media. Answers C and D are not given – he neither shares his own predictions nor brings up any reasons for the continuous decline.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-5-q32.explanation: AThe author gives a number of examples where various, seemingly outdated media kept on being popular despite anything. Answers B, C and D are not mentioned – in fact, the opposite is stated.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-5-q33.explanation: B‘Withstood’ means ‘was strong enough to resist something or defend against something’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-5-q34.explanation: AThe other three answers mention bits of the paragraph, whereas answer A covers the general idea of the paragraph – it is important for people to comprehend the importance of change in their perception, without which any progress is going to be difficult to make.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-5-q35.explanation: AParagraph Four hails the ease with which online newspapers can post, update and bring news to their readership. The flexibility is indeed the key aspect throughout the paragraph. The rest of the answer only partially cover the points made by the author.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-5-q36.explanation: A‘.. they and they alone’ in the last paragraph refer to the newspapers and how they are contrasted to the news websites on the Internet.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-6-q37.explanation: AParagraph C voices concerns about the falling numbers of visitors to the smaller museums which are unable to compete with the bigger ones in keeping their online materials up to date. However, in Paragraph A the author states the opposite, last sentence: ‘… I know of many such museums all over the country which are thriving’ referring to the smaller museums (see previous sentence).

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-6-q38.explanation: DBoth directors approve of the idea to exchange museum exhibits: Last sentence of Paragraph B and last sentence of Paragraph D.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-6-q39.explanation: CParagraph A’s writer is convinced that small local museums can still be very popular (last sentence). However, in Paragraph C the opposite is stated: ‘… provincial museums lose out to the large nationals, as their more limited resources mean they cannot hope to compete.’

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-6-q40.explanation: DUnlike opinions voiced in other paragraphs, in D the writer is still convinced that museums pose real interest to few people, and there is still a lot of work to do to attract ‘visitors from less privileged backgrounds’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-7-q41.explanation: GThe paragraph opens up with the suggestion to make use of all that lost heat. ‘Recapturing it’ at the beginning of the following paragraph refers to the leaking heat, mentioned at the end of Paragraph G.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-7-q42.explanation: B‘An attractive proposition’ mentioned at the beginning of Paragraph B refers to the ‘next energy revolution’ part at the end of the previous paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-7-q43.explanation: DA number of paragraphs fits this gap, but it is the ending of Paragraph D that helps connect it to the following one, with the explanation of the suggested alternative system that exploits heat to warm houses and water.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-7-q44.explanation: CThere’s a phrase ‘ What’s more, it’s barely warm enough to merit its name.’ in the bottom part of Paragraph C that helps us connect it with the beginning of the following paragraph: ‘… there is an existing technology that can siphon energy from such temperatures…’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-7-q45.explanation: EPumps mentioned in the previous paragraph help us to choose Paragraph E which elaborates and expands on the idea of heat pumps that make use of the ground warmth.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-7-q46.explanation: FParagraph F beings with ‘While this is not what you might consider hot…’ which refers to the 10-degree warmth mentioned in the previous paragraph. The concluding paragraph goes on the explain how the system can be benefitted from.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q47.explanation: CSecond sentence of this paragraph states: ‘… boredom has a definite evolutionary purpose.’. The author then carries on to substantiate this claim by an example of what we’d be like if we didn’t allow ourselves to get bored occasionally.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q48.explanation: DThe middle of the paragraph mentions the author turning off his phone on the weekends.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q49.explanation: BSecond sentence of Paragraph B: ‘… It’s a beautiful theory and one that would definitely hold an allure for many people.’

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q50.explanation: AThe middle of the paragraph mentions a thinker, who came to realise ‘several decades ago’ that boredom can be beneficial to us.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q51.explanation: DSecond sentence of this paragraph makes it clear that ‘pondering’ and purposefully avoiding any activity are different things.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q52.explanation: CLast sentence of the paragraph gives an example of incorrect lessons that we give to our children, how boredom is something bad, whereas as it turns out it can be quite useful.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q53.explanation: AThe complicated phrasing of the question can be misleading. Simply put, we need to find a mention of some activity that is common nowadays and takes place everywhere. What the author implies is the use of various electronic devices such as mp3 players and smartphones. See sentence one of this paragraph.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q54.explanation: DIn the second part of Paragraph D the author mentions turning off their mobile phone for the weekend and how they find the effect profoundly beneficial. Their mind becomes ‘refreshed and revitalized’.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q55.explanation: B‘Modern research’ mentioned in the third sentence of this paragraph is the ‘particular finding’ from the task.

catalog-reading-cae-c1-test13-part-8-q56.explanation: CSecond sentence of Paragraph C: ‘… boredom has a definite evolutionary purpose.’.
